english: How can I act thus? Someone might perhaps see us, and then misfortune would befall you as well as me.

sanskrit: tasmānmadhūtsavākṣiptapauraloke gṛhaṃ mama / āgantavaṃ dhruvaṃ rātreḥ prathame prahare tvayā // ityuktvā kṛtasaṃdhā sā tena kṣipta vidhervaśāt / yāvatkiṃcidgatā tāvanniruddhā sā purodhasā //
english: Therefore you must come without fail to my house in the first watch of the night of the spring festival when the citizens are all excited.”[7] When she had said this, and pledged herself, he let her go, but, as chance would have it, she had not gone many steps farther before she was stopped by the king’s domestic priest.

sanskrit: tasyāpi tatraiva dine tadvadeva tayā niśi / saṃketakaṃ dvitīyasmin prahare paryakalpyata //
english: She made a similar assignation with him also for the second watch of the same night; and so he too was, though with difficulty, induced to let her go;

sanskrit: atha tasyāpi divase tasminneva tathaiva sā / saṃketakaṃ triyāmāyāṃ tṛtīye prahare vyadhāt // daivāttenāpi nirmuktā sakampā gṛhamāgatā / kartavyāṃ sā svaceṭīnāṃ saṃvidaṃ svairamabravīt // varaṃ patyau pravāsasthe maraṇaṃ kulayoṣitaḥ / na tu rūpāramallokalocanāpātapātratā // iti saṃcintayantī ca smarantī māṃ nināya sā / śocantī svaṃ vapuḥ sādhvī nirāhāraiva tāṃ niśām //
english: but after she had gone a little farther, up comes a third person, the head magistrate, and detains the trembling lady. Then she made a similar assignation with him too for the third watch of the same night, and having by great good fortune got him to release her, she went home all trembling, and of her own accord told her handmaids the arrangements she had made, reflecting: “Death is better for a woman of good family, when her husband is away, than to meet the eyes of people who lust after beauty.” Full of these thoughts, and regretting me, the virtuous lady spent that night in fasting, lamenting her own beauty.

sanskrit: prātarbrāhmaṇapūjārthaṃ vyasarji vaṇijastayā / ceṭī hiraṇyaguptasya kiṃcinmārgayituṃ dhanam //
english: Early the next morning she sent a maid-servant to the merchant Hiraṇyagupta to ask for some money in order that she might honour the Brāhmans;

sanskrit: āgatyā so 'pi tāmevamekānte vaṇirābravīt / bhajasva māṃ tato bhartṛsthāpitaṃ te dadāmi tat // tacchrutvā sākṣirahitāṃ matvā bhartṛdhanasthitim / vaṇijaṃ pāpamālokya khedāmarṣakadarthitā // tasyāmevātra saṃketaṃ rātrau tasyāpi paścime / śeṣe pativratā yāme sākarodatha so 'gamat //
english: then that merchant also came and said to her in private: “Show me love, and then I will give you what your husband deposited.” When she heard that, she reflected that she had no witness to prove the deposit of her husband’s wealth, and perceived that the merchant was a villain, and so, tortured with sorrow and grief, she made a fourth and last assignation with him for the last watch of the same night;

sanskrit: tataḥ sākārayadbhūri ceṭībhiḥ kuṇḍakasthitam / kastūrikādisaṃyuktaṃ kajjalaṃ tailamiśritam // talliptāścelakhaṇḍāśca catvāro vihitāstayā / mañjūṣā kāritā cābhutsthūlā sabahirargalā //
english: In the meanwhile she had prepared by her handmaids in a large vat lamp-black mixed with oil and scented with musk and other perfumes, and she made ready four pieces of rag anointed with it, and she caused to be made a large trunk with a fastening outside.

sanskrit: atha tasminmahāveṣo vasantotsavavāsare / āyayau prathame yāme kumārasacivo niśi //
english: So on that day of the spring festival the prince’s minister came in the first watch of the night in gorgeous array.

sanskrit: alakṣitaṃ praviṣṭaṃ tamupakośedamabravīt / asnātaṃ na spṛśāmi tvāṃ tatsnāhi praviśāntaram //
english: When he had entered without being-observed, Upakośā said to him: “I will not receive you until you have bathed, so go in and bathe.” The simpleton agreed to that, and was taken by the handmaids into a secret dark inner apartment.

sanskrit: aṅgīkurvansa tanmūḍhaśceṭikābhiḥ praveśitaḥ / abhyantaragṛhaṃ guptamandhakāramayaṃ tataḥ // gṛhītvā tatra tasyāntarvastrāṇyābharaṇāni ca / celakhaṇḍaṃ tamekaṃ ca dattvāntarvāsasaḥ kṛte //
english: There they took off his undergarments and his jewels, and gave him by way of an undergarment a single piece of rag, and they smeared the rascal from head to foot with a thick coating of that lamp-black and oil, pretending it was an unguent, without his detecting it.

sanskrit: atiṣṭhanmardayantyastatpratyaṅgaṃ yāvadasya tāḥ / tāvaddvitīye prahare sa purodhā upāgamat // mittraṃ vararuceḥ prāptaḥ kimapyeṣa purohitaḥ / tadiha praviśetyuktvā ceṭyastāstaṃ tathāvidham // kumārasacivaṃ nagnaṃ mañjūṣāyāṃ sasaṃbhramam / nicikṣipurathābadhnannargalena bahiśca tām //
english: While they continued rubbing it into every limb the second watch of the night came and the priest arrived. The handmaids thereupon said to the minister: “Here is the king’s priest come, a great friend of Vararuci’s, so creep into this box,” and they bundled him into the trunk just as he was, all naked, with the utmost precipitation; and then they fastened it outside with a bolt.

sanskrit: so 'pi snānamiṣānnītastamasyantaḥ purohitaḥ / tathaiva hṛtavastrādistailakajjalamardanaiḥ // celakhaṇḍadharastāvacceṭikābhirvimohitaḥ / yāvattṛtīye prahare daṇḍādhipatirāgamat //
english: The priest too was brought inside into the dark room on the pretence of a bath, and was in the same way stripped of his garments and ornaments, and made a fool of by the handmaids by being rubbed with lamp-black and oil, with nothing but the piece of rag on him, until in the third watch the chief magistrate arrived.

sanskrit: tadāgamanajāccaiva ceṭībhiḥ sahasā bhayāt / ādyavatso 'pi nikṣipto mañjūṣāyāṃ purohitaḥ //
english: The handmaids immediately terrified the priest with the news of his arrival, and pushed him into the trunk like his predecessor.

sanskrit: tasya dattvārgalaṃ tābhiḥ snānavyājāt praveśya saḥ / daṇḍādhipo 'pi tatraiva tāvatkajjalamardanaiḥ // anyavadvipralabdho 'bhūccelakhaṇḍaikakarpaṭaḥ / yāvatsa paścime yāme vaṇiktatrāgato 'bhavat // taddarśanabhayaṃ dattvā kṣipto daṇḍādhipo 'pyatha / mañjūṣāyāṃ sa ceṭībhirdattaṃ ca bahirargalam //
english: After they had bolted him in, they brought in the magistrate on the pretext of giving him a bath, and so he, like his fellows, with a piece of rag for his only garment, was bamboozled by being continually anointed with lamp-black, until in the last watch of the night the merchant arrived. The handmaids made use of his arrival to alarm the magistrate, and bundled him also into the trunk and fastened it on the outside.

sanskrit: te ca trayo 'ndhatāmisravasabhyāsodyatā iva / mañjūṣāyāṃ bhiyānyonyaṃ sparśaṃ labdhvāpi nālapan //
english: So those three being shut up inside the box, as if they were bent on accustoming themselves to live in the hell of blind darkness, did not dare to speak on account of fear, though they touched one another.

sanskrit: dattvātha dīpaṃ gehe 'tra vaṇijaṃ taṃ praveśya sā / upakośāvadaddehi tanme bhartrārpitaṃ dhanam // tacchrutvā śūnyamālokya gṛhaṃ so 'pyavadacchaṭhaḥ / uktaṃ mayā dadāmyeva yadbhartrā sthāpitaṃ dhanam // upakośāpi mañjūṣāṃ śrāvayantī tato 'bravīt / etaddhiraṇyaguptasya vacaḥ śṛṇuta devatāḥ // ity uktvā caiva nirvāpya dīpaṃ so 'py anyavadvaṇik / liptaḥ snānāpadeśena ceṭībhiḥ kajjalaiś ciram //
english: Then Upakośā brought a lamp into the room, and making the merchant enter it, said to him: “Give me that money which my husband deposited with you.” When he heard that, the rascal said, observing that the room was empty: “I told you that I would give you the money your husband deposited with me.” Upakośā, calling the attention of the people in the trunk, said: “Hear, O ye gods, this speech of Hiraṇyagupta.” When she had said this she blew out the light, and the merchant, like the others, on the pretext of a bath, was anointed by the handmaids for a long time with lamp-black.

sanskrit: atha gaccha gatā rātrir ity uktaḥ sa niśākṣaye / anicchan galahastena tābhir nirvāsitas tataḥ //
english: Then they told him to go, for the darkness was over, and at the close of the night they took him by the neck and pushed him out of the door sorely against his will.

sanskrit: atha cīraikavasano maṣīliptaḥ pade pade / bhakṣyamāṇaḥ śvabhiḥ prāpa lajjamāno nijaṃ gṛham //
english: Then he made the best of his way home, with only the piece of rag to cover his nakedness, and smeared with the black dye, with the dogs biting him at every step, thoroughly ashamed of himself, and at last reached his own house;

sanskrit: tatra dāsajanasyāpi tāṃ prakṣālayato maṣīm / nāśakatsaṃmukhe sthātuṃ kaṣṭo hyavinayakramaḥ //
english: and when he got there he did not dare to look his slaves in the face while they were washing off that black dye.

sanskrit: upakośāpy atha prātaś ceṭikānugatā gatā / gurūṇām anivedyaiva rājño nandasya mandiram // vaṇigghiraṇyagupto me bhartrā nyāsīkṛtaṃ dhanam / jihīrṣatīti vijñaptas tatra rājā tayā svayam //
english: In the early morning Upakośā, accompanied by her handmaids, went, without informing her parents, to the palace of King Nanda, and there she herself stated to the king that the merchant Hiraṇyagupta was endeavouring to deprive her of money deposited with him by her husband.

sanskrit: tena tac ca parijñātuṃ tatraivānāyito vaṇik / maddhaste kiṃcid apy asyā deva nāstīty abhāṣata //
english: The king, in order to inquire into the matter, immediately had the merchant summoned, who said: “I have nothing in my keeping belonging to this lady.” Upakośā then said: “I have witnesses, my lord;

sanskrit: upakośā tato 'vādītsanti me deva sākṣiṇaḥ / mañjūṣāyāṃ gataḥ kṣiptvā bhartā me gṛhadevatāḥ // svavācā puratastāsāmanenāṅgīkṛtaṃ dhanam / tāmānāyyeha mañjūṣāṃ pṛcchyantāṃ devatāstvayā //
english: before he went, my husband put the household gods into a box, and this merchant with his own lips admitted the deposit in their presence. Let the box be brought here and ask the gods yourself.” Having heard this, the king in astonishment ordered the box to be brought.

sanskrit: tacchrutvā vismayādrājā tadānayanamādiśat / tataḥ kṣaṇāt sā mañjūṣā prāpitā bahubhirjanaiḥ //
english: Thereupon in a moment that trunk was carried in by many men.

sanskrit: athopakośā vakti sma satyaṃ vadata devatāḥ / yaduktaṃ vaṇijānena tato yāta nijaṃ gṛham //
english: Then Upakośā said: “Relate truly, O gods, what that merchant said, and then go to your own houses;

sanskrit: no ceddadāmyahaṃ yuṣmānsadasyudghāṭayāmi vā / tacchrutvā bhītabhītāste mañjūṣāsthā babhāṣire // satyaṃ samakṣam asmākam anenāṅgīkṛtaṃ dhanam / tato niruttaraḥ sarvaṃ sa vaṇik tat prapadyata //
english: if you do not, I will burn you or open the box in court.” Hearing that, the men in the box, beside themselves with fear, said: “It is true, the merchant admitted the deposit in our presence.” Then the merchant, being utterly confounded, confessed all his guilt;

sanskrit: upakośāmathābhyarthya rājñā tvatikutūhalāt / sadasyudghāṭitā tatra mañjūṣā sphoṭitārgalā // niṣkṛṣṭāste 'pi puruṣāstamaḥ piṇḍā iva trayaḥ / kṛcchrācca pratyabhijñātā mantribhirbhūbhṛtā tathā //
english: but the king, being unable to restrain his curiosity, after asking permission of Upakośā, opened the chest there in court by breaking the fastening, and those three men were dragged out, looking like three lumps of solid darkness, and were with difficulty recognised by the king and his ministers.

sanskrit: prahasatsvatha sarveṣu kimetaditi kautukāt / rājñā pṛṣṭā satī sarvamupakośā śaśaṃsa tat //
english: The whole assembly then burst out laughing, and the king in his curiosity asked Upakośā what was the meaning of all this;

sanskrit: acintyaṃ śīlaguptānāṃ caritaṃ kulayoṣitām / iti cābhinanandustāmupakośāṃ sabhāsadaḥ // tatas te hṛtasarvasvāḥ paradāriṣiṇo 'khilāḥ / rājñā nirvāsitā deśādaśīlaṃ kasya bhūtaye //
english: All present in court expressed their approbation of Upakośā’s conduct, observing: “The virtuous behaviour of women of good family who are protected by their own excellent disposition[8] only, is incredible.” Then all those coveters of their neighbour’s wife were deprived of all their living, and banished from the country.

sanskrit: bhaginī me tvamityuktvā dattvā prītyā dhanaṃ bahu / upakośāpi bhūpena preṣitā gṛhamāgamat //
english: Who prospers by immorality? Upakośā was dismissed by the king, who showed his great regard for her by a present of much wealth, and said to her: “Henceforth thou art my sister”; and so she returned home.

sanskrit: varṣopavarṣau tadbuddhvā sādhvīṃ tāmabhyanandatām / sarvaśca vismayasmeraḥ pure tatrābhavajjanaḥ //
english: Varṣa and Upavarṣa, when they heard it, congratulated that chaste lady, and there was a smile of admiration on the face of every single person in that city.

sanskrit: atrāntare tuṣārādrau kṛtvā tīvrataraṃ tapaḥ / ārādhito mayā devo varadaḥ pārvatīpatiḥ //
english: In the meanwhile, by performing a very severe penance on the snowy mountain, I propitiated the god, the husband of Pārvatī, the great giver of all good things;

sanskrit: tadeva tena śāstraṃ me pāṇinīyaṃ prakāśitam / tadicchānugrahādeva mayā pūrṇīkṛtaṃ ca tat //
english: he revealed to me that same treatise of Pāṇini;

sanskrit: tato 'haṃ gṛham āgaccham ajñātādhvapariśramaḥ / niśākarakalāmauliprasādāmṛtanirbharaḥ //
english: and in accordance with his wish I completed it: then I returned home without feeling the fatigue of the journey, full of the nectar of the favour of that god who wears on his crest a digit of the moon;

sanskrit: atha mātur gurūṇāṃ ca kṛtapādābhivandanaḥ / tatropakośāvṛttāntaṃ tam aśrauṣaṃ mahādbhutam // tena me paramāṃ bhūmimātmanyānandavismayau / tasyāṃ ca sahajasnehabahumānāvagacchatām //
english: then I worshipped the feet of my mother and of my spiritual teachers, and heard from them the wonderful achievement of Upakośā; thereupon joy and astonishment swelled to the upmost height in my breast, together with natural affection and great respect for my wife.

sanskrit: varṣo 'tha manmukhādaicchacchrotuṃ vyākaraṇaṃ navam / tataḥ prakāśitaṃ svāmikumāreṇaiva tasya tat // tato vyāḍīndradattābhyāṃ vijñapto dakṣiṇāṃ prati / gururvarṣo 'bravīt svarṇakoṭir me dīyatām iti // aṅgīkṛtya gurorvākyaṃ tau ca māmityavocatām / ehi rājñaḥ sakhe nandādyācituṃ gurudakṣiṇām //
english: Now Varṣa expressed a desire to hear from my lips the new grammar, and thereupon the god Kārttikeya himself revealed it to him. And it came to pass that Vyāḍi and Indradatta asked their preceptor Varṣa what fee they should give him. He replied: “Give me ten millions of gold pieces.” So they, consenting to the preceptor’s demand, said to me: “Come with us, friend, to ask the King Nanda to give us the sum required for our teacher’s fee;

sanskrit: gacchāmo nānyato 'smābhiriyatkāñcanamāpyate / navādhikāyā navateḥ koṭīnāmadhipo hi saḥ // vācā tenopakośā ca prāgdharmabhaginī kṛtā / ataḥ śyālaḥ sa te kiṃcittvadguṇaiḥ samavāpyate //
english: we cannot obtain so much gold from any other quarter: for he possesses nine hundred and ninety millions, and so long ago he declared your wife Upakośā his sister in the faith, therefore you are his brother-in-law;

sanskrit: iti niścitya nandasya bhūpateḥ kaṭakaṃ vayam / ayodhyāsthamagacchāma trayaḥ sabrahmacāriṇaḥ // prāptamātreṣu cāsmāsu sa rājā pañcatāṃ gataḥ / rāṣṭre kolāhalaṃ jātaṃ viṣādena sahaiva naḥ //
english: we shall obtain something for the sake of your virtues.” Having formed this resolution, we three fellow-students[9] went to the camp of King Nanda in Ayodhyā, and the very moment we arrived the king died; accordingly an outburst of lamentation arose in the kingdom, and we were reduced to despair.

sanskrit: avocadindradatto 'tha tatkṣaṇaṃ yogasiddhimān / gatāsorasya bhūpasya śarīraṃ praviśāmyaham //
english: Immediately Indradatta, who was an adept in magic, said: “I will enter the body of this dead king [see notes on the entering of another’s body];

sanskrit: arthī vararucirme 'stu dāsyāmyasmai ca kāñcanam / vyāḍī rakṣatu me dehaṃ tataḥ pratyāgamāvadhi // ityuktvā nandadehāntarindradattaḥ samāviśat / pratyujjīvati bhūpe ca rāṣṭre tatrotsavo 'bhavat //
english: let Vararuci prefer the petition to me, and I will give him the gold, and let Vyāḍi guard my body until I return.” Saying this, Indradatta entered into the body of King Nanda, and when the king came to life again there was great rejoicing in the kingdom.

sanskrit: śūnye devagṛhe dehamindradattasya rakṣitum / vyāḍau sthite gato 'bhūvamahaṃ rājakulaṃ tadā //
english: While Vyāḍi remained in an empty temple to guard the body of Indradatta, I went to the king’s palace.

sanskrit: praviśya svastikāraṃ ca vidhāya gurudakṣiṇām / yoganando mayā tatra hemakoṭiṃ sa yācitaḥ //
english: I entered, and, after making the usual salutation, I asked the supposed Nanda for ten million gold pieces as my instructor’s fee.

sanskrit: tataḥ sa śakaṭālākhyaṃ satyanandasya mantriṇam / suvarṇakoṭimetasmai dāpayeti samādiśat //
english: Then he ordered a man named Śakatāla,[10] the minister of the real Nanda, to give me ten million of gold pieces.

sanskrit: mṛtasya jīvitaṃ dṛṣṭvā sadyaśca prāptimarthinaḥ / sa tattvaṃ jñātavānmantrī kimajñeyaṃ hi dhīmatām //
english: That minister, when he saw that the dead king had come to life, and that the petitioner immediately got what he asked, guessed the real state of the case.

sanskrit: deva dīyata ityuktvā sa ca mantrītyacintayat / nandasya tanayo bālo rājyaṃ ca bahuśatrumat // tatsaṃpratyatra rakṣāmi tasya dehamapīdṛśam / niścityaitatsa tatkālaṃ śavānsarvānadāhayat // cārairanviṣya tanmadhye labdhvā devagṛhāttataḥ / vyāḍiṃ vidhūya taddagdhamindradattakalevaram //
english: What is there that the wise cannot understand? That minister said: “It shall be given, your Highness,” and reflected with himself: “Nanda’s son is but a child, and our realm is menaced by many enemies, so I will do my best for the present to keep his body on the throne even in its present state.” Having resolved on this, he immediately took steps to have all dead bodies burned, employing spies to discover them, and among them was found the body of Indradatta, which was burned after Vyāḍi had been hustled out of the temple.

sanskrit: atrāntare ca rājānaṃ hemakoṭisamarpaṇe / tvaramāṇamathāha sma śakaṭālo vicārayan // utsavākṣiptacitto 'yaṃ sarvaḥ parijanaḥ sthitaḥ / kṣaṇaṃ pratīkṣatāmeṣa vipro yāvaddadāmyaham //
english: In the meanwhile the king was pressing for the payment of the money, but Śakatāla, who was still in doubt, said to him: “All the servants have got their heads turned by the public rejoicing, let the Brāhman wait a moment until I can give it.” Then Vyāḍi came and complained aloud in the presence of the supposed Nanda: “Help, help;

sanskrit: athaitya yoganandasya vyāḍinā kranditaṃ puraḥ / abrahmaṇyamanutkrāntajīvo yogasthito dvijaḥ // anāthaśava ityadya balāddagdhastavodaye / tacchrutvā yoganandasya kāpyavasthābhavacchucā //
english: a Brāhman engaged in magic, whose life had not yet come to an end in a natural way, has been burnt by force on the pretext that his body was untenanted, and this in the very moment of your good fortune.”[11] On hearing this the supposed Nanda was in an indescribable state of distraction from grief;

sanskrit: dehadāhātsthire tasmiñjāte nirgatya me dadau / suvarṇakoṭiṃ sa tataḥ śakaṭālo mahāmatiḥ //
english: but as soon as Indradatta was imprisoned in the body of Nanda, beyond the possibility of escape, by the burning of his body, the discreet Śakatāla went out and gave me that ten millions.

sanskrit: yoganando 'tha vijane saśoko vyāḍimabravīt / śūdrībhūto 'smi vipro 'pi kiṃ śriyā sthirayāpi me //
english: Then the supposed Nanda,[12] full of grief, said in secret to Vyāḍi: “Though a Brāhman by birth, I have become a Śūdra.

sanskrit: tacchrutvāśvāsya taṃ vyāḍiḥ kālocitamabhāṣata / jñāto 'si śakaṭālena tadenaṃ cintayādhunā // mahāmantrī hyayaṃ svecchamacirāttvāṃ vināśayet / pūrvanandasutaṃ kuryāc candraguptaṃ hi bhūmipam //
english: What is the use of my royal fortune to me though it be firmly established?” When he heard that, Vyāḍi comforted him,[13] and gave him seasonable advice: “You have been discovered by Śakatāla, so you must henceforth be on your guard against him, for he is a great minister, and in a short time he will, when it suits his purpose, destroy you, and will make Candragupta, the son of the previous Nanda, king.

sanskrit: tasmādvararuciṃ mantrimukhyatve kuru yena te / etadbuddhyā bhavedrājyaṃ sthiraṃ divyānubhāvayā // ityuktaiva gate vyāḍau dātuṃ tāṃ gurudakṣiṇām / tadaivānīya dattā me yoganandena mantritā //
english: Therefore immediately appoint Vararuci your minister, in order that your rule may be firmly established by the help of his intellect, which is of god-like acuteness.” When he had said this, Vyāḍi departed to give that fee to his preceptor, and immediately Yogananda sent for me and made me his minister.

sanskrit: athoktaḥ sa mayā rājā brāhmaṇye hārite 'pi te / rājyaṃ naiva sthiraṃ manye śakaṭāle padasthite // tasmānnāśaya yuktyainamiti mantre mayodite / yoganando 'ndhakūpāntaḥ śakaṭālaṃ tamakṣipat // kiṃ ca putraśataṃ tasya tatraiva kṣiptavānasau / jīvandvijo 'munā dagdha iti doṣānukīrtanāt //
english: Then I said to the king: “Though your estate as a Brāhman has been taken from you, I do not consider your throne secure as long as Śakatāla remains in office, therefore destroy him by some stratagem.” When I had given him this advice, Yogananda threw Śakatāla into a dark dungeon,[14] and his hundred sons with him, proclaiming as his crime that he had burnt a Brāhman alive.

sanskrit: ekaḥ śarāvaḥ saktūnāmekaḥ pratyahamambhasaḥ / śakaṭālasya tatrāntaḥ saputrasya nyadhīyata // sa covāca tataḥ putrānamībhiḥ saktubhiḥ sutāḥ / eko 'pi kṛcchrād varteta bahūnāṃ tu kathaiva kā //
english: One porringer of barley-meal and one of water was placed inside the dungeon every day for Śakatāla and his sons, and thereupon he said to them: “My sons, even one man alone would with difficulty subsist on this barley-meal, much less can a number of people do so.

sanskrit: tasmātsaṃbhakṣayatvekaḥ pratyahaṃ sajalānamūn / yaḥ śakto yoganandasya kartuṃ vairapratikriyām // tvameva śakto bhuṅkṣvaitaditi putrāstamabruvan / prāṇebhyo 'pi hi dhīrāṇāṃ priyā śatrupratikriyā //
english: Therefore let that one of us who is able to take vengeance on Yogananda consume every day the barley-meal and the water.” His sons answered him: “You alone are able to punish him, therefore do you consume them.” For vengeance is dearer to the resolute than life itself.

sanskrit: tataḥ sa śakaṭālastaiḥ pratyahaṃ saktuvāribhiḥ / eka evākarod vṛttiṃ kaṣṭaṃ krūrā jigīṣavaḥ //
english: So Śakatāla alone subsisted on that meal and water every day.

sanskrit: abuddhvā cittam aprāpya visrambhaṃ prabhaviṣṇuṣu / na svecchaṃ vyavahartavyam ātmano bhūtim icchatā // iti cācintayat tatra śakaṭālo 'ndhakūpagaḥ / tanayānāṃ kṣudhārtānāṃ paśyan prāṇodgamavyathām // tataḥ sutaśataṃ tasya paśyatastadvyapadyata / tatkaraṅkairvṛto jīvannatiṣṭhatsa ca kevalaḥ //
english: Alas! those whose souls are set on victory are cruel. Śakatāla, in the dark dungeon, beholding the death agonies of his starving sons, thought to himself: “A man who desires his own welfare should not act in an arbitrary manner towards the powerful without fathoming their character and acquiring their confidence.” Accordingly his hundred sons perished before his eyes, and he alone remained alive, surrounded by their skeletons.

sanskrit: yoganandaśca sāmrājye baddhamūlo 'bhavattataḥ / vyāḍirabhyāyayau taṃ ca gurave dattadakṣiṇaḥ // abhyetyaiva ca so 'vādīcciraṃ rājyaṃ sakhe 'stu te / āmantrito si gacchāmi tapastaptumahaṃ kvacit // tacchrutvā yoganandastaṃ bāṣpakaṇṭho 'pyabhāṣata / rājye me bhuṅkṣva bhogāṃstvaṃ bhuktvā māṃ mā sma gā iti //
english: And Vyāḍi approached him after giving the present to his teacher, and after coming near to him said: “May thy rule, my friend, last long! I take my leave of thee. I go to perform austerities somewhere.” Hearing that, Yogananda, with his voice choked with tears, said to him: “Stop thou and enjoy pleasure in my kingdom; do not go and desert me.” Vyāḍi answered: “King! life comes to an end in a moment.

sanskrit: vyāḍis tato 'vadad rājañ śarīre kṣaṇanaśvare / evaṃprāyeṣv asāreṣu dhīmān ko nāma majjati // nahi mohayati prājñaṃ lakṣmīrmarumarīcikā / ityuktvaiva sa tatkālaṃ tapase niścito yayau //
english: What wise man, I pray you, drowns himself in these hollow and fleeting enjoyments? Prosperity, a desert mirage, does not turn the head of the wise man.” Saying this he went away that moment, resolved to mortify his flesh with austerities.

sanskrit: agamad atha yoganandaḥ pāṭaliputraṃ svarājanagaraṃ saḥ / bhogāya kāṇabhūte matsahitaḥ sakalasainyayutaḥ //
english: Then that Yogananda went to his metropolis, Pāṭaliputra, for the purpose of enjoyment, accompanied by me, and surrounded with his whole army.

sanskrit: tatropakośāparicaryamāṇaḥ samudvahanmantridhurāṃ ca tasya / ahaṃ jananyā gurubhiś ca sākam āsādya lakṣmīmavasaṃ cirāya //
english: So I, having attained prosperity, lived for a long time in that state, waited upon by Upakośā, and bearing the burden of the office of prime minister to that king, accompanied by my mother and my preceptors.

sanskrit: bahu tatra dine dine dyusindhuḥ kanakaṃ mahyamadāttapaḥ prasannā / vadati sma śarīriṇī ca sākṣān mama kāryāṇi sarasvatī sadaiva //
english: There the Ganges, propitiated by my austerities, gave me every day much wealth, and Sarasvatī, present in bodily form, told me continually what measures to adopt.

sanskrit: iti mahākaviśrīsomadevabhaṭṭaviracite kathāsaritsāgare kathāpīṭhalambake caturthas taraṅgaḥ / pañcamas taraṅgaḥ / evamuktvā vararuciḥ punaretadavarṇayat / kālena yoganando 'tha kāmādivaśamāyayau // gajendra iva mattaśca nāpaikṣata sa kiṃcana / akāṇḍapātopanatā kaṃ na lakṣmīr vimohayet //
english: [Additional note: The “entrapped suitors” motif] [M] (main story line continued) HAVING said this, Vararuci continued his tale as follows: — In course of time Yogananda became enslaved by his passions, and like a mad elephant he disregarded every restraint.

sanskrit: acintayaṃ tataścāhaṃ rājā tāvadviśṛṅkhalaḥ / tatkāryacintayākrāntaḥ svadharmo me 'vasīdati // tasmādvaraṃ sahāyaṃ taṃ śakaṭālaṃ samuddhare / kriyetā cedviruddhaṃ ca kiṃ da kuryānmayi sthite // niścityaitanmayābhyarthya rājānaṃ so 'ndhakūpataḥ / uddhṛtaḥ śakaṭālo 'tha mṛdavo hi dvijātayaḥ //
english: Whom will not a sudden access of prosperity intoxicate? Then I reflected with myself: “The king has burst all bonds, and my own religious duties are neglected, being interfered with by my care for his affairs, therefore it is better for me to draw out that Śakatāla from his dungeon and make him my colleague in the ministry; even if he tries to oppose me, what harm can he do as long as I am in office?” Having resolved on this, I asked permission of the king, and drew Śakatāla out of the deep dungeon.

sanskrit: durjayo yoganando 'yaṃ sthite vararucāvataḥ / āśraye vaitasīṃ vṛttiṃ kālaṃ tāvatpratīkṣitum // iti saṃcintya sa prājñaḥ śakaṭālo madicchayā / akarodrājakāryāṇi punaḥ saṃprāpya mantritām //
english: Now the discreet Śakatāla made up his mind that it would be difficult to overthrow Yogananda as long as I was in office, and that he had accordingly better imitate the cane which bends with the current, and watch a favourable moment for vengeance, so at my request he resumed the office of minister and managed the king’s affairs.

sanskrit: kadācidyoganando 'tha nirgato nagarādvahiḥ / śliṣyatpañcāṅguliṃ hastaṃ gaṅgāmadhye vyalokayat //
english: Once on a time Yogananda went outside the city, and beheld in the middle of the Ganges a hand, the five fingers of which were closely pressed together.

sanskrit: kimetaditi papraccha māmāhūya sa tatkṣaṇam / ahaṃ ca dve nijāṅgulyau diśi tasyāmadarśayam //
english: That moment he summoned me and said: “What does this mean?” But I displayed two of my fingers in the direction of the hand.

sanskrit: tena tasmiṃstirobhūte haste rājātivismayāt / bhūyo 'pi tadapṛcchanmāṃ tataścāhaṃ tamabravam // pañcabhirmilitaiḥ kiṃ yajjagatīha na sādhyate / ityuktavānasau hastaḥ śvāṅgulīḥ pañca darśayan // tato 'sya rājan naṅgulyāv ete dve darśite mayā / aikacitye dvayoreva kimasādhyaṃ bhavediti // ityukte gūḍhavijñāne samatuṣyattato nṛpaḥ / śakaṭālo vyaṣīdacca madbuddhiṃ vīkṣya durjayām //
english: Thereupon that hand disappeared, and the king, exceedingly astonished, again asked me what this meant, and I answered him: “That hand meant to say, by showing its five fingers: ‘What cannot five men united effect in this world?’ Then I, king, showed it these two fingers, wishing to indicate that nothing is impossible when even two men are of one mind.” When I uttered this solution of the riddle the king was delighted, and Śakatāla was despondent, seeing that my intellect would be difficult to circumvent.[1] One day Yogananda saw his queen leaning out of the window and asking questions of a Brāhman guest that was looking up.

sanskrit: tanmātrādeva kupito rājā viprasa tasya saḥ / ādiśadbadhamīrṣyā hi vivekaparipanthinī //
english: That trivial circumstance threw the king into a passion, and he gave orders that the Brāhman should be put to death for jealousy interferes with discernment.

sanskrit: hantuṃ vadhyabhuvaṃ tasmin nīyamāne dvije tadā / ahasadgatajīvo 'pi matsyo vipaṇimadhyagaḥ //
english: Then as that Brāhman was being led off to the place of execution in order that he might be put to death, a fish in the market laughed aloud, though it was dead.

sanskrit: tadaiva rājā tadbuddhvā vadhaṃ tasya nyavārayat / viprasya māmapṛcchacca matsyahāsasya kāraṇam //
english: [also see notes on the motif of laughter] The king hearing it immediately prohibited for the present the execution of that Brāhman, and asked me the reason why the fish laughed.

sanskrit: nirūpya kathayāmyetadityuktvā nirgataṃ ca mām / cintitopasthitaikānte sarasvatyevamabravīt // asya tālataroḥ pṛṣṭhe tiṣṭha rātrābalakṣitaḥ / atra śroṣyasi matsyasya hāsahetum asaṃśayam // tacchrutvā niśi tatrāhaṃ gatvā tālopari sthitaḥ / apaśyaṃ rākṣasīṃ ghorāṃ bālaiḥ putraiḥ sahāgatam //
english: and after I had gone out Sarasvatī came to me secretly on my thinking of her and gave me this advice: “Take up a position on the top of this palm-tree at night so as not to be observed, and thou shalt without doubt hear the reason why the fish laughed.” Hearing this I went at night to that very place, and ensconced myself on the top of the palm-tree, and saw a terrible female Rākṣasa[2] coming past with her children;

sanskrit: sā bhakṣyaṃ yācamānāṃstānavādītpratipālyatām / prātarvo vipramāṃsāni dāsyāmyadya hato na saḥ //
english: when they asked her for food, she said: “Wait, and I will give you to-morrow morning the flesh of a Brāhman;

sanskrit: kasmātsa na hato 'dyeti pṛṣṭā tairabravītpunaḥ / taṃ hi dṛṣṭva mṛto 'pīha matsyo hasitavāniti // hasitaṃ kimu teneti pṛṣṭā bhūyaḥ sutaiśca sā / avocadrākṣasī rājñaḥ sarvā rājño 'pi viplutāḥ // sarvatrāntaḥpure hyatra strīrūpāḥ puruṣāḥ sthitāḥ / hanyate 'naparādhas tu vipra ity ahasat timiḥ //
english: he was not killed to-day.”[3] They said to their mother: “Why was he not killed today?” Then she replied: “He was not executed because a fish in the town, though dead, laughed when it saw him.” The sons said: “Why did the fish laugh?” She continued: “The fish, of course, said to himself: ‘All the king’s wives are dissolute, for in every part of this harem there are men dressed up as women, and nevertheless while these escape an innocent Brāhman is to be put todeath,’ and this tickled the fish so that he laughed.

sanskrit: bhūtānāṃ pārthivātyarthanirvivekatvahāsinām / sarvāntaścāriṇāṃ hyetā bhavantyeva ca vikriyāḥ // etattasyā vacaḥ śrutvā tato 'pakrāntavāhanam / prāptaśca matsyahāsasya hetuṃ rājñe nyavedayam //
english: For demons assume these disguises, insinuating themselves into everything, and laughing at the exceeding want of discernment of kings.” After I had heard that speech of the female Rākṣasa I went away from thence, and in the morning I informed the king why the fish laughed.

sanskrit: prāpya cāntaḥpurebhyas tān strīrūpān puruṣāṃs tataḥ / bahv amanyata māṃ rājā vadhādvipraṃ ca muktavān //
english: The king, after detecting in the harem those men clothed as women, looked upon me with great respect, and released that Brāhman from the sentence of death.

sanskrit: ityādi ceṣṭitaṃ dṛṣṭvā tasya rājño viśṛṅkhalam / khinne mayi kadācicca tatrāgāccitrakṛnnavaḥ //
english: I was disgusted by seeing this and other lawless proceedings on the part of the king, and while I was in this frame of mind there came to the Court a new painter.

sanskrit: alikhat sa mahādevīṃ yoganandaṃ ca taṃ paṭe / sajīvam iva taccitraṃ vākceṣṭārahitaṃ tv abhūt //
english: He painted on a sheet of canvas the principal queen and Yogananda, and that picture of his looked as if it were alive; it only lacked speech and motion.

sanskrit: taṃ ca citrakaraṃ rājā tuṣṭo vittairapūrayat / taṃ ca vāsagṛhe citrapaṭaṃ bhittāvakārayat //
english: And the king, being delighted, loaded that painter with wealth, and had the painting set up on a wall in his private apartments.

sanskrit: ekadā ca praviṣṭasya vāsake tatra sā mama / saṃpūrṇalakṣaṇā devī pratibhāti sma citragā //
english: Now one day when I entered into the king’s private apartments it occurred to me that the painting of the queen did not represent all her auspicious marks;

sanskrit: lakṣaṇāntarasaṃbandhādabhyūhya pratibhāvaśāt / athākārṣamahaṃ tasyāstilakaṃ mekhalāpade //
english: from the arrangement of the other marks I conjectured by means of my acuteness that there ought to be a spot where the girdle comes, and I painted one there.

sanskrit: saṃpūrṇalakṣaṇāṃ tena kṛtvaināṃ gatavānaham / praviṣṭo yoganando 'tha tilakaṃ taṃ vyalokayat //
english: Then I departed after thus giving the queen all her lucky marks. Then Yogananda entered and saw that spot, and asked his chamberlains who had painted it.

sanskrit: kenāyaṃ racito 'treti so 'pṛcchacca mahattarān / te ca nyavedayaṃstasmai kartāraṃ tilakasya mām //
english: And they indicated me as the person who had painted it.

sanskrit: devyā guptapradeśasthamimaṃ nānyo mayā vinā / vetti tajjñātavānevamasau vararuciḥ katham // channaḥ kṛto 'munā nūnaṃ mamāntaḥpuraviplavaḥ / dṛṣṭavānata evāyaṃ strīrūpāṃstatra tānnarān // iti saṃcintayāmāsa yoganandaḥ krudhā jvalan / jāyante bata mūḍhānāṃ saṃvāda api tādṛśāḥ // tataḥ svairaṃ samāhūya śakaṭālaṃ samādiśat / tvayā vararucirvadhyo devīvidhvaṃsanāditi // yathā jñāpayasītyuktvā śakaṭālo 'gamadbahiḥ / acintayacca śaktiḥ syāddhantuṃ vararuciṃ na me //
english: Yogananda thus reflected while burning with anger: “No one except myself knows of that spot, which is in a part of the queen’s body usually concealed, then how can this Vararuci have come thus to know it?[4] No doubt he has secretly corrupted my harem, and this is how he came to see there those men disguised as women.” Foolish men often find such coincidences.[5] Then of his own motion he summoned Śakatāla, and gave him the following order:— “You must put Vararuci to death for seducing the queen.” Śakatāla said: “Your Majesty’s orders shall be executed,” and went out of the palace, reflecting: “I should not have power to put Vararuci to death, for he possesses god-like force of intellect;

sanskrit: divyabuddhiprabhāvo 'sābuddhartā ca mamāpadaḥ / viprasya tadvaraṃ guptaṃ saṃprati svīkaromi tam //
english: and he delivered me from calamity; moreover he is a Brāhman;

sanskrit: iti niścitya so 'bhyetya rājñaḥ kopamakāraṇam / vadhāntaṃ kathayitvā me śakaṭālo 'bravīttataḥ // anyaṃ kaṃcitpravādāya hanmyahaṃ tvaṃ ca madgṛhe / pracchannas tiṣṭha mām asmād rakṣituṃ kopanān nṛpāt // iti tadvacanāc channas tadgṛhe 'vasthito 'bhavam / sa cānyaṃ hatavān kaṃcin madvadhākhyātaye niśi // evaṃ prayuktanītiṃ taṃ prītyāvocamahaṃ tadā / eko mantrī bhavānyena hantuṃ māṃ na kṛtā matiḥ //
english: therefore I had better hide him and win him over to my side.” Having formed this resolution, he came and told me of the king’s causeless wrath which had ended in his ordering my execution, and thus concluded: “I will have someone else put to death in order that the news may get abroad, and do you remain hidden in my house to protect me from this passionate king.” In accordance with this proposal of his, I remained concealed in his house, and he had someone else put to death at night, in order that the report of my death might be spread.[6] When he had in this way displayed his statecraft, I said to him out of affection: “You have shown yourself an unrivalled minister in that you did not attempt to put me to death;

sanskrit: nahi hantumahaṃ śakyo rākṣaso mittramasti me / dhyātamātrāgato viśvaṃ grasate sa madicchayā //
english: for I cannot be slain, since I have a Rākṣasa to friend, and he will come, on being only thought of, and at my request will devour the whole world.

sanskrit: rājā tvihendradattākhyaḥ sakhā vadhyo na me dvijaḥ / tacchrutvā so 'bravīnmantrī rakṣo me darśyatāmiti //
english: As for this king, he is a friend of mine, being a Brāhman named Indradatta, and he ought not to be slain.” Hearing this, that minister said: “Show me the Rākṣasa.” Then I showed him that Rākṣasa who came with a thought;

sanskrit: tato dhyātāgataṃ tasmi tadrakṣo 'hamadarśayam / taddarśanācca vitrasto vismitaśca vabhūva saḥ //
english: and on beholding him Śakatāla was astonished and terrified.

sanskrit: rakṣasyantarhite tasmiñ śakaṭālaḥ sa māṃ punaḥ / kathaṃ te rākṣaso mittraṃ saṃjāta iti pṛṣṭavān // tato 'hamavadaṃ pūrvaṃ rakṣārthaṃ nagare bhraman / rātrau rātrau kṣayaṃ prāpadekaiko nagarādhipaḥ //
english: And when the Rākṣasa had disappeared Śakatāla again asked me: “How did the Rākṣasa become your friend?” Then I said: “Long ago the heads of the police, as they went through the city night after night on inspecting duty, perished one by one.

sanskrit: tacchrutvā yoganando māmakaronnagarādhipam / bhramaṃścāpaśyamatrāhaṃ bhramantaṃ rākṣasaṃ niśi // sa ca māmavadadbrūhi vidyate nagare 'tra kā / surūpā strīti tacchrutvā vihasyāhaṃ tamabravam // yā yasyābhimatā mūrkha surūpā tasya sā bhavet / tacchrutvaiva tvayaikena jito 'smītyavadatsa mām //
english: On hearing that, Yogananda made me head of the police, and as I was on my rounds at night I saw a Rākṣasa roaming about, and he said to me: ‘Tell me, who is considered the best-looking woman in this city?’ When I heard that I burst out laughing, and said: ‘You fool, any woman is good-looking to the man who admires her.’ Hearing my answer, he said: ‘You are the only man that has beaten me.’ And now that I had escaped death by solving his riddle,[7] he again said to me: ‘I am pleased with you;

sanskrit: praśnamokṣādvadhottirṇaṃ māṃ punaścābravīdasau / tuṣṭo 'smīti suhṛnme tvaṃ saṃnidhāsye ca te smṛtaḥ //
english: henceforth you are my friend, and I will appear to you when you call me to mind.’ Thus he spoke and disappeared, and I returned by the way that I came.

sanskrit: ityuktvāntarhite tasminyathāgatamagāmaham / evam āpatsahāyo me rākṣaso mittratāṃ gataḥ // ityuktavānahaṃ bhūyaḥ śakaṭālena cārthitaḥ / gaṅgāmadarśayaṃ tasmai mūrtāṃ dhyānādupasthitām //
english: Thus the Rākṣasa has become my friend, and my ally in trouble.” When I had said this, Śakatāla made a second request to me, and I showed him the goddess of the Ganges in human form who came when I thought of her.

sanskrit: stutibhistoṣitā sā ca mayā devī tirodadhe / babhūva śakaṭālaśca sahāyaḥ praṇato mayi //
english: And that goddess disappeared when she had been gratified by me with hymns of praise. But Śakatāla became from henceforth my obedient ally.

sanskrit: ekadā ca sa mantrī māṃ guptasthaṃ khinnamabravīt / sarvajñenāpi khedāya kimātmā dīyate tvayā // kiṃ na jānāsi yadrājñāmavicāraratā dhiyaḥ / acirācca bhavecchuddhistathā cātra kathaṃ śṛṇu // ādityavarmanāmātra babhūva nṛpatiḥ purā / śivavarmābhidhāno 'sya mantrī cābhūnmahāmatiḥ //
english: Now once on a time that minister said to me when my state of concealment weighed upon my spirits: “Why do you, although you know all things, abandon yourself to despondency? Do you not know that the minds of kings are most undiscerning, and in a short time you will be cleared from all imputations?[8] In proof of which listen to the following tale:— There reigned here long ago a king named Ādityavarman, and he had a very wise minister, named Śivavarman.

sanskrit: rājñastasyaikadā caikā rājñī garbhamadhārayat / tadbuddhvā sa nṛpo 'pṛcchadityantaḥ purarakṣiṇaḥ // varṣadvayaṃ praviṣṭasya vartate 'ntaḥpure 'tra me / tadeṣā garbhasaṃbhūtiḥ kutaḥ saṃprati kathyatām // athocuste praveśo 'tra puṃso 'nyasyāsti na prabho / śivavarmā tu te mantrī praviśatyanivāritaḥ // tacchrutvācintayadrājā nūnaṃ drohī sa eva me / prakāśaṃ ca hate tasminnapavādo bhavenmama // ityālocya sa taṃ yuktyā śivavarmāṇamīśvaraḥ / sāmantasyāntikaṃ sakhyuḥ prāhiṇodbhogavarmaṇaḥ //
english: Now it came to pass that one of that king’s queens became pregnant, and when he found it out, the king said to the guards of the harem: “It is now two years since I entered this place, then how has this queen become pregnant? Tell me.” Then they said: “No man except your minister Śivavarman is allowed to enter here, but he enters without any restriction.” When he heard that, the king thought: “Surely he is guilty of treason against me, and yet if I put him to death publicly I shall incur reproach.” Thus reflecting, that king sent that Śivavarman on some pretext to Bhogavarman, a neighbouring chief,[9] who was an ally of his, and immediately afterwards the king secretly sent off a messenger to the same chief, bearing a letter by which he was ordered to put the minister to death.[10] When a week had elapsed after the minister’s departure, that queen tried to escape out of fear, and was taken by the guards with a man in woman’s attire.

sanskrit: ādityavarmā tadbuddhvā sānutāpo 'bhavattadā / kiṃ mayā tādṛśo mantrī ghātito 'kāraṇāditi //
english: Then Ādityavarman when he heard of it was filled with remorse, and asked himself why he had causelessly brought about the death of so excellent a minister.

sanskrit: atrāntare sa ca prāpa nikaṭaṃ bhogavarmaṇaḥ / śivavarmā sa copāgāllekhamādāya pūruṣaḥ // vācayitvā ca taṃ lekhamekānte śivavarmaṇe / śaśaṃsa vadhanirdeśaṃ bhogavarmā vidhervaśāt //
english: In the meanwhile Śivavarman reached the Court of Bhogavarman, and that messenger came bringing the letter; and fate would have it so that after Bhogavarman had read the letter he told to Śivavarman in secret the order he had received to put him to death.

sanskrit: śivavarmāpy avocat taṃ sāmantaṃ mantrisattamaḥ / tvaṃ vyāpādaya māṃ no cen nihanmyātmānam ātmanā // tacchrutvā vismayāviṣṭo bhogavarmā jagāda tam / kimetadbrūhi me vipra śāpito 'si na vakṣi cet //
english: The excellent minister Śivavarman in his turn said to that chief: “Put me to death; if you do not, I will slay myself with my own hand.” When he heard that, Bhogavarman was filled with wonder, and said to him: “What does all this mean? Tell me, Brāhman;

sanskrit: atha vakti sma taṃ mantrī hanyeyaṃ yatra bhūpate / tatra dvādaśa varṣāṇi deśe devo na varṣati // tacchrutvā mantribhiḥ sārdhaṃ bhogavarmā vyacintayat / duṣṭaḥ sa rājā deśasya nāśamasmākamicchati // kiṃ hi tatra na santyeva vadhakā guptagāminaḥ / tasmānmantrī na vadhyo 'sau rakṣyaḥ svātmavadhādapi //
english: if you do not, you will lie under my curse.” Then the minister said to him: “King, in whatever land I am slain, on that land God will not send rain for twelve years.” When he heard that, Bhogavarman debated with his minister: “That wicked king desires the destruction of our land, for could he not have employed secret assassins to kill his minister? So we must not put this minister to death.

sanskrit: iti saṃmantrya dattvā ca rakṣakān bhogavarmaṇā / śivavarmā tato deśāt preṣito 'bhūt tataḥ kṣaṇāt //
english: Moreover, we must prevent him from laying violent hands on himself.” Having thus deliberated and appointed him guards, Bhogavarman sent Śivavarman out of his country that moment;

sanskrit: evaṃ pratyāyayau jīvansa mantrī prajñayā svayā / śuddhiścāsyānyato jātā nahi dharmo 'nyathā bhavet //
english: so that minister by means of his wisdom returned alive, and his innocence was established from another quarter, for righteousness cannot be undone.

sanskrit: itthaṃ tavāpi śuddhiḥ syāttiṣṭha tāvadgṛhe mama / kātyāyana nṛpo 'pyeṣa sānutāpo bhaviṣyati //
english: In the same way your innocence will be made clear, Kātyāyana[11]; remain for a while in my house; this king too will repent of what he has done.

sanskrit: ityuktaḥ śakaṭālena cchanno 'haṃ tasya veśmani / pratīkṣamāṇo 'vasaraṃ tānyahānyatyavāhayam //
english: When Śakatāla said this to me, I spent those days concealed in his house.

sanskrit: tasyātha yoganandasya kāṇabhūteḥ kadācana / putro hiraṇyaguptākhyo mṛgayāyai gato 'bhavat // aśvavegātprayātasya kathaṃciddūramantaram / ekākino vane tasya vāsaraḥ paryahīyata //
english: Then it came to pass that one day, O Kāṇabhūti, a son of that Yogananda named Hiraṇyagupta went out hunting, and when he had somehow or other been carried to a great distance by the speed of his horse, while he was alone in the wood, the day came to an end;

sanskrit: tataśca tāṃ niśāṃ netuṃ vṛkṣamārohati sma saḥ / kṣaṇāttatraiva cārohadṛkṣaḥ siṃhena bhīṣitaḥ //
english: and then he ascended a tree to pass the night. Immediately afterwards a bear, which had been terrified by a lion, ascended the same tree;

sanskrit: sa dṛṣṭvā rājaputraṃ taṃ bhītaṃ mānuṣabhāṣayā / mā bhaiṣīrmama mittraṃ tvamityuktvā nirbhayaṃ vyadhāt //
english: he seeing the prince frightened, said to him with a human voice: “Fear not, thou art my friend,” and thus promised him immunity from harm.

sanskrit: visrambhādṛkṣavākyena rājaputro 'tha suptavān / ṛkṣastu jāgradevāsīdadhaḥ siṃho 'tha so 'bravīt //
english: Then the prince, confiding in the bear’s promise, went to sleep, while the bear remained awake.

sanskrit: ṛkṣaṃ mānuṣametaṃ me kṣipa yāvadvrajāmyaham / ṛkṣastato 'bravītpāpa na mitraṃ ghātayāmyaham // kramādṛkṣe prasupte ca rājaputre ca jāgrati / punaḥ siṃho 'bravīdetamṛkṣaṃ me kṣipa mānuṣa // tacchrutvātmabhayāttena siṃhasyārādhanāya saḥ / kṣipto 'pi nāpataccitramṛkṣo daivaprabodhitaḥ //
english: Then the lion below said to the bear: “Bear, throw me down this man and I will go away.” Then the bear said: “Villain, I will not cause the death of a friend.” When in course of time the bear went to sleep while the prince was awake, the lion said again: “Man, throw me down the bear.” When he heard that, the prince, who through fear for his own safety wished to propitiate the lion, tried to throw down the bear, but, wonderful to say, it did not fall, since fate caused it to awake.

sanskrit: mittradrohin bhavonmatta iti śāpam adāc ca saḥ / tasya rājasutasyaitadvṛttāntāvagamāvadhim //
english: And then that bear said to the prince: “Become insane, thou betrayer of thy friend,”[12] laying upon him a curse destined not to end until a third person guessed the whole transaction.

sanskrit: prāpyaiva svagṛhaṃ prātarunmatto 'bhūnnṛpātmajaḥ / yoganandaśca taddṛṣṭvā viṣādaṃ sahasāgamat //
english: Accordingly the prince, when he reached his palace in the morning, went out of his mind, and Yogananda seeing it was immediately plunged in despondency, and said;

sanskrit: abravīcca sa kāle 'smiñ jīved vararucir yadi / idaṃ jñāyeta tatsarvaṃ dhiṅ me tadvadhapāṭavam //
english: “If Vararuci were alive at this moment all this matter would be known;

sanskrit: tacchrutvā vacanaṃ rājñaḥ śakaṭālo vyacintayat / hanta kātyāyanasyāyaṃ labdhaḥ kālaḥ prakāśane // na so 'tra mānī tiṣṭheca rājā mayi ca viśvaset / ityālocya sa rājānamabravīdyācitābhayaḥ //
english: curse on my readiness to have him put to death!” Śakatāla, when he heard this exclamation of the king’s, thought to himself: “Ha! here is an opportunity obtained for bringing Kātyāyana out of concealment, and he, being a proud man, will not remain here, and the king will repose confidence in me.” After reflecting thus, he implored pardon, and said to the king: “O King, cease from despondency;

sanskrit: rājannalaṃ viṣādena jīvanvararuciḥ sthitaḥ / yoganandastato 'vādīddrutamānīyatāmiti // athāhaṃ śakaṭālena yoganandāntikaṃ haṭhāt / ānītas taṃ tathābhūtaṃ rājaputraṃ vyalokayam //
english: Vararuci remains alive.” Then Yogananda said: “Let him be brought quickly.” Then I was suddenly brought by Śakatāla into the presence of Yogananda and beheld the prince in that state;

sanskrit: mittradrohaḥ kṛto 'nena devetyuktvā tathaiva saḥ / sarasvatīprasādena vṛttāntaḥ kathito mayā // tatastacchāpamuktena stuto 'haṃ rājasūnunā / tvayā kathamidaṃ jñātamityapṛcchatsa bhūpatiḥ //
english: and by the favour of Sarasvatl I was enabled to reveal the whole occurrence; and I said: “King, he has proved a traitor to his friend.” Then I was praised by that prince who was delivered from his curse; and the king asked me how I had managed to find out what had taken place.

sanskrit: athāham avadaṃ rājaṃl lakṣaṇair anumānataḥ / pratibhātaśca paśyanti sarvaṃ prajñāvatāṃ dhiyaḥ //
english: Then I said: “King, the minds of the wise see everything by inference from signs, and by acuteness of intellect.

sanskrit: tadyathā tilako jñātastathā sarvamidaṃ mayā / iti madvacanātso 'bhūdrājā lajjānutāpavān //
english: So I found out all this in the same way as I found out that mole.” When I had said this, that king was afflicted with shame.

sanskrit: athānādṛtasatkāraḥ pariśuddhyaiva lābhavān / svagṛhaṃ gatavānasmi śīlaṃ hi viduṣāṃ dhanam //
english: Then, without accepting his munificence, considering myself to have gained all I desired by the clearing of my reputation, I went home; for to the wise character is wealth.

sanskrit: prāptasyaiva ca tatratyo jano 'rodītpuro mama / abhyetya māṃ samudbhrāntamupavarṣo 'bravīttataḥ // rājā hataṃ niśamya tvāmupakośāgnisādvapuḥ / akarodatha mātuste śucā hṛdayamasphuṭat // tac chrutvābhinavodbhūtaśokāvegavicetanaḥ / sadyo 'ham apataṃ bhūmau vātarugṇa iva drumaḥ //
english: And the moment I arrived the servants of my house wept before me, and when I was distressed at it Upavarṣa came to me and said: “Upakośā, when she heard that the king had put you to death, committed her body to the flames,[13] and then your mother’s heart broke with grief.” Hearing that, senseless with the distraction produced by recently aroused grief, I suddenly fell on the ground like a tree broken by the wind; and in a moment I tasted the relief of loud lamentations.

sanskrit: kṣaṇācca gatavānasmi pralāpānāṃ rasajñatām / priyabandhuvināśotthaḥ śokāgniḥ kaṃ na tāpayet // ā saṃsāraṃ jagatyasminnekā nityā hyanityatā / tadetāmaiśvarīṃ māyāṃ kiṃ jānannapi muhyasi // ityādibhir upāgatya varṣeṇa vacanair aham / bodhito 'tha yathātattvaṃ kathaṃciddhṛtimāptavān //
english: Whom will not the fire of grief, produced by the loss of dear relations, scorch? Varṣa came and gave me sound advice in such words as these: “The only thing that is stable in this ever-changeful world is instability; then why are you distracted though you know this delusion of the Creator?” By the help of these and similar exhortations I at length, though with difficulty, regained my equanimity;

sanskrit: tato viraktahṛdayastyaktvā sarvaṃ nibandhanam / praśamaikasahāyo 'haṃ tapovanamaśiśriyam //
english: then, with heart disgusted with the world, I flung aside all earthly lords and, choosing self-restraint for my only companion, I went to a grove where asceticism was practised.

sanskrit: divaseṣvatha gacchatsu tattapovanamekadā / ayodhyāta upāgacchadvipra eko mayi sthite //
english: Then, as days went by, once on a time a Brāhman from Ayodhyā came to that ascetic grove while I was there.

sanskrit: sa mayā yoganandasya rājyavārtām apṛcchyata / pratyabhijñāya māṃ so 'tha saśokamidamabravīt // śṛṇu nandasya yadvṛttaṃ tatsakāśādgate tvayi / labdhvāvakāśas tatrābhūc chakaṭālaś cireṇa saḥ //
english: I asked him for tidings about Yogananda’s government, and he recognising me told me in sorrowful accents the following story:— “Hear what happened to Nanda after you had left him. Śakatāla, after waiting for it a long time, found that he had now obtained an opportunity of injuring him.

sanskrit: sa cintayanvadhopāyaṃ yoganandasya yuktitaḥ / kṣitiṃ khanantamadrākṣīccāṇakyākhyaṃ dvijaṃ pathi //
english: While thinking how he might by some device get Yogananda killed, he happened to see a Brāhman named Cāṇakya digging up the earth in his path.

sanskrit: kiṃ bhuvaṃ khanasītyukte tena vipro 'tha so 'bravīt / darbhamunmūlayāmyatra pādo hyetena me kṣataḥ // tacchrutvā sahasā mantrī kopanaṃ krūraniścayam / taṃ vipraṃ yoganandasya vadhopāyamamanyata // nāma pṛṣṭvābravīttaṃ ca he brahmandāpayāmi te / ahaṃ trayodaśīśrāddhaṃ gṛhe nandasya bhūpateḥ //
english: He said to him: ‘Why are you digging up the earth?’ The Brāhman whom he had asked said: ‘I am rooting up a plant of darbha grass here because it has pricked my foot.[14] When he heard that, the minister thought that Brāhman who formed such stern resolves out of anger would be the best instrument to destroy Nanda with.’ After asking his name he said to him: ‘Brāhman, I assign to you the duty of presiding at a śrāddha [also see notes on śrāddha] on the thirteenth day of the lunar fortnight, in the house of King Nanda;

sanskrit: dakṣiṇātaḥ suvarṇasya lakṣaṃ tava bhaviṣyati / bhokṣyase dhuri cānyeṣāmehi tāvadgṛhaṃ mama //
english: you shall have one hundred thousand gold pieces by way of fee, and you shall sit at the board above all others;

sanskrit: ityuktvā śakaṭālastaṃ cāṇakyamanayadgṛham / śrāddhāhe 'darśayattaṃ ca rājñe sa śraddadhe ca tam //
english: in the meanwhile come to my house.’ Saying this, Śakatāla took that Brāhman to his house, and on the day of the śrāddha he showed the Brāhman to the king, and he approved of him.

sanskrit: tataḥ sa gatvā cāṇakyo dhuri śrāddha upāviśat / subandhunāmā vipraśca tāmaicchaddhuramātmanaḥ //
english: Then Cāṇakya went and sat at the head of the table during the śrāddha, but a Brāhman named Subandhu desired that post of honour for himself.

sanskrit: tadgatvā śakaṭālena vijñapto nandabhūpatiḥ / avādīnnāparo yogyaḥ subandhurdhuri tiṣṭhatu // āgatyaitāṃ ca rājājñāṃ śakaṭālo bhayānataḥ / na me 'parādha ityuktvā cāṇakyāya nyavedayat // so 'tha kopena cāṇakyo jvalanniva samantataḥ / nijāṃ muktvā śikhāṃ tatra pratijñāmakarodimām // avaśyaṃ hanta nando 'yaṃ saptabhirdivasairmayā / vināśyo bandhanīyā ca tato nirbhanyunā śikhā //
english: Then Śakatāla went and referred the matter to King Nanda, who answered: ‘Let Subandhu sit at the head of the table; no one else deserves the place.’ Then Śakatāla went and, humbly bowing through fear, communicated that order of the king’s to Cāṇakya, adding: ‘It is not my fault.’ Then that Cāṇakya, being, as it were, inflamed all over with wrath, undoing the lock of hair on the crown of his head, made this solemn vow: ‘Surely this Nanda must be destroyed by me within seven days, and then my anger being appeased I will bind up my lock.’[15] When he had said this, Yogananda was enraged;

sanskrit: ityuktavantaṃ kupite yoganande palāyitam / alakṣitaṃ svagehe taṃ śakaṭālo nyaveśayat //
english: so Cāṇakya escaped unobserved and Śakatāla gave him refuge in his house.

sanskrit: tatropakaraṇe datte guptaṃ tenaiva mantriṇā / sa cāṇakyo dvijaḥ kvāpi gatvā kṛtyāmasādhayat //
english: Then, being supplied by Śakatāla with the necessary instruments, that Brāhman Cāṇakya went somewhere and performed a magic rite;

sanskrit: tadvaśādyoganando 'tha dāhajvaramavāpya saḥ / saptame divase prāpte pañcatvaṃ samupāgamat //
english: in consequence of this rite Yogananda caught a burning fever, and died when the seventh day arrived;

sanskrit: hatvā hiraṇyaguptaṃ ca śakaṭālena tatsutam / pūrvanandasute lakṣmīścandragupte niveśitā //
english: and Śakatāla, having slain Nanda’s son Hiraṇyagupta, bestowed the royal dignity upon Candragupta, a son of the previous Nanda.

sanskrit: mantritve tasya cābhyarthya bṛhaspatisamaṃ dhiyā / cāṇakyaṃ sthāpayitvā taṃ sa mantrī kṛtakṛtyatām // manvāno yoganandasya kṛtavairapratikriyaḥ / putraśokena nirviṇṇaḥ praviveśa mahadvanam // iti tasya mukhācchrutvā viprasya sutarāmaham / kāṇabhūte gataḥ khedaṃ sarvamālokya cañcalam //
english: And after he had requested Cāṇakya, equal in ability to Bṛhaspati,[16] to be Candragupta’s prime minister and established him in the office, that minister, considering that all his objects had been accomplished, as he had wreaked his vengeance on Yogananda, despondent through sorrow for the death of his sons, retired to the forest.”[17] After I had heard this, O Kāṇabhūti, from the mouth of that Brāhman, I became exceedingly afflicted, seeing that all things are unstable;

sanskrit: khedāc cāham imāṃ draṣṭum āgato vindhyavāsinīm / tatprasādena dṛṣṭvā tvāṃ smṛtā jātirmayā sakhe //
english: and on account of my affliction I came to visit this shrine of Durgā, and through her favour having beheld you, O my friend, I have remembered my former birth.

sanskrit: prāptaṃ divyaṃ ca vijñānaṃ mayoktā te mahākathā / idānīṃ kṣīṇaśāpo 'haṃ yatiṣye dehamujjhitum //
english: And having obtained divine discernment I have told you the great tale. Now, as my curse has spent its strength, I will strive to leave the body;

sanskrit: tvaṃ ca saṃprati tiṣṭheha yāvadāyāti te 'ntikam / śiṣyayukto guṇāḍhyākhyastyaktabhāṣātrayo dvijaḥ // so 'pi hyahamiva krodhāddevyā śapto gaṇottamaḥ / mālyavānnāma matpakṣapātī martyatvamāgataḥ //
english: and do you remain here for the present, until there comes to you a Brāhman named Guṇāḍhya, who has forsaken the use of three languages,[18] surrounded with his pupils, for he like myself was cursed by the goddess in anger, being an excellent Gaṇa, Mālyavān by name, who for taking my part has become a mortal.

sanskrit: tasmai maheśvaroktaiṣā kathanīyā mahākathā / tataste śāpanirmuktistasya cāpi bhaviṣyati //
english: To him you must tell this tale originally told by Śiva, then you shall be delivered from your curse, and so shall he.

sanskrit: evaṃ vararucistatra kāṇabhūternivedya saḥ / pratasthe dehamokṣāya puṇyaṃ badarikāśramam //
english: [M] (main story line continued) Having said all this to Kāṇabhūti, that Vararuci set forth for the holy hermitage of Badarikā in order to put off his body.

sanskrit: gacchandadarśa gaṅgāyāṃ so 'tha śākāśinaṃ munim / tatsamakṣaṃ ca tasyarṣeḥ kuśenābhūtkarakṣatiḥ //
english: As he was going along he beheld on the banks of the Ganges a vegetable-eating[19] hermit, and while he was looking on, that hermit’s hand was pricked with kuśa grass.

sanskrit: tato 'sya rudhiraṃ niryattena śākarasīkṛtam / ahaṃkāraparīkṣārthaṃ kautukātsvaprabhāvataḥ //
english: Then Vararuci turned his blood, as it flowed out, into sap[20] through his magic power, out of curiosity, in order to test his egotism;

sanskrit: taddṛṣṭvā hanta siddho 'smītyagāddarpamasau muniḥ / tato vararuciḥ kiṃcidvihasyeva jagāda tam //
english: on beholding that, the hermit exclaimed: “Ha! I have attained perfection”; and so he became puffed up with pride.

sanskrit: jijñāsanāya raktaṃ te mayā śākarasīkṛtam / yāvannādyāpyahaṃkāraḥ parityaktastvayā mune //
english: Then Vararuci laughed a little and said to him: “I turned your blood into sap in order to test you, because even now, O hermit, you have not abandoned egotism.

sanskrit: jñānamārge hyahaṃkāraḥ parigho duratikramaḥ / jñānaṃ vinā ca nāstyeva mokṣo vrataśatairapi //
english: Egotism is in truth an obstacle in the road to knowledge hard to overcome, and without knowledge liberation cannot be attained even by a hundred vows.

sanskrit: svargastu na mumukṣūṇāṃ kṣayī cittaṃ vilobhayet / tasmādahaṃkṛtityāgājjñāne yatnaṃ mune kuru //
english: But the perishable joys of Svarga cannot attract the hearts of those who long for liberation;

sanskrit: vinīyaivaṃ muniṃ tena praṇatena kṛtastutiḥ / taṃ badaryāśramoddeśaṃ śāntaṃ vararuciryayau // atha sa nibiḍabhaktyā tatra devīṃ śaraṇyāṃ śaraṇamupagato 'sau martyabhāvaṃ mumukṣuḥ / prakaṭitanijamūrtiḥ sāpi tasmai śaśaṃsa svayamanalasamutthāṃ dhāraṇāṃ dehamuktyai // dagdhvā śarīramatha dhāraṇayā tayā taddivyāṃ gatiṃ vararuciḥ sa nijāṃ prapede / vindhyāṭavībhuvi tataḥ sa ca kāṇabhūtir āsīdabhīpsitaguṇāḍhyasamāgamotkaḥ //
english: therefore, O hermit, endeavour to acquire knowledge by forsaking egotism.” Having thus read that hermit a lesson, and having been praised by him prostrate in adoration, Vararuci went to the tranquil site of the hermitage of Badarī.[21] There he, desirous of putting off his mortal condition, resorted for protection with intense devotion to that goddess who only can protect, and she, manifesting her real form to him, told him the secret of that meditation which arises from fire, to help him to put off the body. Then Vararuci, having consumed his body by that form of meditation, reached his own heavenly home;

sanskrit: iti mahākaviśrīsomadevabhaṭṭaviracite kathāsaritsāgare kathāpīṭhalambake pañcamas taraṅgaḥ / ṣaṣṭhas taraṅgaḥ / tataḥ sa martyavapuṣā mālyavānvicaranvane / nāmnā guṇāḍhaḥ sevitvā sātavāhanabhūpatim // saṃskṛtādyāstadagre ca bhāṣāstisraḥ pratijñayā / tyaktvā khinnamanā draṣṭumāyayau vindhyavāsinīm //
english: and henceforth that Kāṇabhūti remained in the Vindhya forest, eager for his desired meeting with Guṇāḍhya. [M] (main story line continued) THEN that Mālyavān wandering about in the wood in human form, passing under the name of Guṇāḍhya, having served the King Sātavāhana, and having, in accordance with a vow, abandoned in his presence the use of Sanskrit and two other languages, with sorrowful mind came to pay a visit to Durgā, the dweller in the Vindhya hills;

sanskrit: tadādeśena gatvā ca kāṇabhūtiṃ dadarśa saḥ / tato jātiṃ nijāṃ smṛtvā prabuddhaḥ sahasābhavat //
english: and by her orders he went and beheld Kāṇabhūti. Then he remembered his origin and suddenly, as it were, awoke from sleep;

sanskrit: āśritya bhāṣāṃ paiśācīṃ bhāṣātrayavilakṣaṇām / śrāvayitvā nijaṃ nāma kāṇabhūtiṃ ca so 'bravīt // puṣpadantācchrutāṃ divyāṃ śīghraṃ kathaya me kathām / yena śāpaṃ tariṣyāvas tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca samaṃ sakhe // tacchrutvā praṇato hṛṣṭaḥ kāṇabhūtiruvāca tam / kathayāmi kathāṃ kiṃ tu kautukaṃ me mahatprabho //
english: and making use of the Paiśācha language, which was different from the three languages he had sworn to forsake, he said to Kāṇabhūti, after telling him his own name: “Quickly tell me that tale which you heard from Puṣpadanta, in order that you and I together, my friend, may escape from our curse.” Hearing that, Kāṇabhūti bowed before him, and said to him in joyful mood: “I will tell you the story, but great curiosity possesses me, my lord;

sanskrit: ājanmacaritaṃ tāvacchaṃsa me kurvanugraham / iti tenārthito vaktuṃ guṇāḍhyo 'tha pracakrame //
english: do me this favour.” Thus being entreated by him, Guṇāḍhya proceeded to relate as follows:— In Pratiṣṭhāna[1] there is a city named Supratiṣṭhita;

sanskrit: vatsaś ca gulmakaś caiva tasya dvau tanayau sakhe / jāyete sma tṛtīyā ca śrutārthā nāma kanyakā // kālena brāhmaṇaḥ so 'tha sabhāryaḥ pañcatāṃ gataḥ / tatputrau tau svasāraṃ tāṃ pālayantāvatiṣṭhatām //
english: in it there dwelt once upon a time an excellent Brāhman named Somaśarman, and he, my friend, had two sons, Vatsa and Gulma, and he had also born to him a third child, a daughter named Śrutārthā. Now in course of time that Brāhman and his wife died, and those two sons of his remained, taking care of their sister.

sanskrit: sā cākasmātsagarbhābhūttadṛṣṭvā vatsagulmayoḥ / tatrānyapuruṣābhāvācchaṅkānyonyamajāyata // tataḥ śrutārthā cittajñā bhrātarau tāvabhāṣata / pāpaśaṅkā na kartavyā śṛṇutaṃ kathayāmi vām //
english: And she suddenly became pregnant. Then Vatsa and Gulma began to suspect one another, because no other man came in their sister’s way: thereupon Śrutārthā, who saw what was in their minds, said to those brothers: “Do not entertain evil suspicions: listen, I will tell you the truth.

sanskrit: kumāraḥ kīrtisenākhyo nāgarājasya vāsukeḥ / bhrātuḥ putro 'sti tenāhaṃ dṛṣṭā snātuṃ gatā satī //
english: There is a prince of the name of Kīrtisena, brother’s son to Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas[2];

sanskrit: tataḥ sa madanākrānto nivedyānvayanāmanī / gāndharveṇa vivāhena māṃ bhāryāmakarottadā //
english: he saw me when I was going to bathe, thereupon he was overcome with love, and after telling me his lineage and his name, made me his wife by the gāndharva marriage[3];

sanskrit: viprajāterayaṃ tasmānmama garbha iti svasuḥ / śrutvā kaḥ pratyayo 'treti vatsagulmāvavocatām // tato rahasi sasmāra sā taṃ nāgakumārakam / smṛtamātrāgataḥ so 'tha vatsagulmāvabhāṣata // bhāryā kṛtā mayaiveyaṃ śāpabhraṣṭā varāpsarāḥ / yuṣmatsvasā yuvāṃ caiva śāpenaiva cyutau bhuvi //
english: he belongs to the Brāhman race, and it is by him that I am pregnant.” When they heard this speech of their sister’s, Vatsa and Gulma said: “What confidence can we repose in all this?” Then she silently called to mind that Nāga prince, and immediately he was thought upon he came and said to Vatsa and Gulma: “In truth I have made your sister my wife.

sanskrit: putro janiṣyate cātra yuṣmatsvasurasaṃśayam / tato 'syāḥ śāpanirmuktiryuvayośca bhaviṣyati // ityuktvāntarhitaḥ so 'bhūttataḥ stokaiśca vāsaraiḥ / śrutārthāyāḥ suto jātastaṃ hi jānīhi māṃ sakhe //
english: but a son shall without fail be born to your sister here, and then you and she together shall be freed from your curse.” Having said this, he disappeared, and in a few days from that time a son was born to Śrutārthā.

sanskrit: gaṇāvatāro jāto 'yaṃ guṇāḍhyo nāma brāhmaṇaḥ / iti tatkālam udabhūd antarikṣāt sarasvatī // kṣīṇaśāpāstataste ca jananīmātulā mama / kālena pañcatāṃ prāptā gataścāhamadhīratām //
english: Know me, my friend, as that son.[4] At that very time a divine voice was heard from heaven: “This child that is born is an incarnation of virtue,[5] and he shall be called Guṇāḍhya,[6] and is of the Brāhman caste.” Thereupon my mother and uncles, as their curse had spent its force, died, and I for my part became inconsolable.

sanskrit: atha śokaṃ samutsṛjya bālo 'pi gatavānaham / svāvaṣṭambhena vidyānāṃ prāptaye dakṣiṇāpatham //
english: Then I flung aside my grief, and though a child I went in the strength of my self-reliance to the Deccan to acquire knowledge.

sanskrit: kālena tatra saṃprāpya sarvā vidyāḥ prasiddhimān / svadeśam āgato 'bhūvaṃ darśayiṣyan nijān guṇān //
english: Then, having in course of time learned all the sciences, and become famous, I returned to my native land to exhibit my accomplishments;

sanskrit: praviśaṃśca cirāttatra nagare supratiṣṭhite / apaśyaṃ śiṣyasahitaḥ śobhāṃ kāmapyahaṃ tadā //
english: and when I entered after a long absence into the city of Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded by my disciples, I saw a wonderfully splendid scene.

sanskrit: kvacitsāmāni chandogā gāyanti ca yathāvidhi / kvacidvivādo viprāṇāmabhūdvedavinirṇaye //
english: In one place chanters were intoning according to prescribed custom the hymns of the Sāma Veda; in another place Brāhmans were disputing about the interpretation of the sacred books;

sanskrit: yo 'tra dyūtakalāṃ vetti tasya hastagato nidhiḥ / ityādikaitavair dyūtam astuvan kitavāḥ kvacit // anyonyaṃ nijavāṇijyakalākauśalavādinām / kvacicca vaṇijāṃ madhye vaṇigeko 'bravīdidam // arthaiḥ saṃyamavān arthān prāpnoti kiyad adbhutam / mayā punar vinaivārthaṃ lakṣmīr āsāditā purā //
english: in another place gamblers were praising gambling in these deceitful words “Whoever knows the art of gambling has a treasure in his grasp”; and in another place, in the midst of a knot of merchants, who were talking to one another about their skill in the art of making money, a certain merchant spoke as follows: — “It is not very wonderful that a thrifty man should acquire wealth by wealth; but I long ago achieved prosperity without any wealth to start with.

sanskrit: garbhasthasya ca me pūrvaṃ pitā pañcatvamāgataḥ / manmātuśca tadā pāpairgotrajaiḥ sakalaṃ hṛtam //
english: My father died before I was born, and then my mother was deprived by wicked relations of all she possessed.

sanskrit: tataḥ sā tadbhayād gatva rakṣaṇtī garbham ātmanaḥ / tasthau kumāradattasya pitṛmitrasya veśmani // tatra tasyāśca jāto 'haṃ sādhvyā vṛttinibandhanam / tataścāvardhayatsā māṃ kṛcchakarmāṇi kurvatī //
english: Then she fled through fear of them, watching over the safety of her unborn child, and dwelt in the house of Kumāradatta, a friend of my father’s, and there the virtuous woman gave birth to me, who was destined to be the means of her future maintenance; and so she reared me up by performing menial drudgery.

sanskrit: vaṇikputro 'si tatputra vāṇijyaṃ kuru sāṃpratam / viśākhilākhyo deśe 'smin vaṇik cāsti mahādhanaḥ // daridrāṇāṃ kulīnānāṃ bhāṇḍamūlyaṃ dadāti saḥ / gaccha yācasva taṃ mūlyamiti mātābravīcca mām //
english: And as she was so poor, she persuaded a teacher by way of charity to give me some instruction in writing and ciphering.[8] Then she said to me: ‘You are the son of a merchant, so you must now engage in trade, and there is a very rich merchant in this country called Viśākhila;

sanskrit: mūṣako dṛśyate yo 'yaṃ gataprāṇo 'tra bhūtale / etenāpi hi paṇyena kuśalo dhanamarjayet //
english: he is in the habit of lending capital to poor men of good family;

sanskrit: dattāstava punaḥ pāpa dīnārā bahavo mayā / dūre tiṣṭhatu tadvṛddhistvayā te 'pi na rakṣitāḥ // tacchrutvā sahasaivāhaṃ tamavocaṃ viśākhilam / gṛhīto 'yaṃ mayā tvatto bhāṇḍamulyāya mūṣakaḥ // ityuktvā mūṣakaṃ haste gṛhītvā saṃpuṭe ca tam / likhitvāsya gato 'bhūvam ahaṃ so 'py ahasad vaṇik // caṇakāñjaliyugmena mūlyenā sa ca mūṣakaḥ / mārjārasya kṛte dattaḥ kasyacidvaṇijo mayā //
english: go and entreat him to give you something to start with.’ Then I went to his house, and he, at the very moment I entered, said in a rage to some merchant’s son: ‘You see this dead mouse here upon the floor, even that is a commodity by which a capable man would acquire wealth, but I gave you, you good-for-nothing fellow, many dinars,[9] and so far from increasing them, you have not even been able to preserve what you got.’ When I heard that, I suddenly said to that Viśākhila: ‘I hereby take from you that mouse as capital advanced.’ Saying this I took the mouse up in my hand, and wrote him a receipt for it, which he put in his strong-box, and off I went.

sanskrit: kṛtvā tāṃś caṇakān bhṛṣṭān gṛhītvā jalakumbhikām / atiṣṭhaṃ catvare gatvā chāyāyā nagarādvahiḥ // tatra śrāntāgatāyāmbhaḥ śītalaṃ caṇakāṃśca tān / kāṣṭhabhārikasaṃghāya sapraśrayamadāmaham //
english: Well, I sold that mouse to a certain merchant as cat’s-meat for two handfuls of gram, then I ground up that gram and, taking a pitcher of water, I went and stood on the cross-road in a shady place, outside the city; there I offered with the utmost civility the water and gram to a band of wood-cutters[10];

sanskrit: ekaikaḥ kāṣṭhikaḥ prītyā kāṣṭhe dve dve dadau mama / cikrītavānahaṃ tāni nītvā kāṣṭhāni cāpaṇe // tataḥ stokena mūlyena krītvā tāṃścaṇakāṃstataḥ / tathaiva kāṣṭhikebhyo 'hamanyedyuḥ kāṣṭhamāharam //
english: every wood-cutter gave me as a token of gratitude two pieces of wood; and I took those pieces of wood and sold them in the market; then for a small part of the price which I got for them I bought a second supply of gram, and in the same way on a second day I obtained wood from the wood-cutters.

sanskrit: evaṃ pratidinaṃ kṛtvā prāpya mūlyaṃ kramānyayā / kāṣṭhikebhyo 'khilaṃ dāru krītaṃ tebhyo dinatrayam //
english: Doing this every day I gradually acquired capital, and I bought from those wood-cutters all their wood for three days.

sanskrit: akasmādatha saṃjāte kāṣṭhacchede 'tivṛṣṭibhiḥ / mayā taddāru vikrītaṃ paṇānāṃ bahubhiḥ śataiḥ //
english: Then suddenly there befell a dearth of wood on account of heavy rains, and I sold that wood for many hundred paṇas;

sanskrit: tenaiva vipaṇiṃ kṛtvā dhanena nijakauśalāt / kurvanvaṇijyāṃ kramaśaḥ saṃpanno 'smi mahādhanaḥ //
english: with that wealth I set up a shop and, engaging in traffic, I have become a very wealthy man by my own ability.

sanskrit: sauvarṇo mūṣakaḥ kṛtvā mayā tasmai samarpitaḥ / viśākhilāya so 'pi svāṃ kanyāṃ mahyamadāttataḥ //
english: Then I made a mouse of gold and gave it to that Viśākhila; then he gave me his daughter;

sanskrit: ata eva ca loke 'smin prasiddho mūṣakākhyayā / evaṃ lakṣmīr iyaṃ prāptā nirdhanena satā mayā //
english: and in consequence of my history I am known in the world by the name of Mouse. So without a coin in the world I acquired this prosperity.” All the other merchants then, when they heard this story, were astonished.

sanskrit: tacchrutvā tatra te 'bhūvanvaṇijo 'nye savismayāḥ / dhīrna citrīyate kasmādabhittau citrakarmaṇā // kvacitpratigrahaprāptahemamāṣāṣṭako dvijaḥ / chandogaḥ kaścidityukto viṭaprāyeṇa kenacit // brāhmaṇyādbhojanaṃ tāvadasti te tattvayāmunā / lokayātrā suvarṇena vaidagdhyāyeha śikṣyatām // ko māṃ śiṣayatītyukte tena mugdhena so 'bravīt / yaiṣā caturikā nāma veśyā tasyā gṛhaṃ vraja //
english: How can the mind help being amazed at pictures without walls?[11] In another place a Brāhman who had got eight gold māṣas[12] as a present, a chanter of the Sāma Veda, received the following piece of advice from a man who was a bit of a roué: — “You get enough to live upon by your position as a Brāhman, so you ought now to employ this gold for the purpose of learning the way of the world in order that you may become a knowing fellow.” The fool said: “Who will teach me?” Thereupon the roué said to him: “This lady,[13] named Caturikā;

sanskrit: tatra kiṃ karavāṇīti dvijenokto viṭo 'bravīt / svarṇaṃ dattvā prayuñjīthā rañjayansāma kiṃcana // śrutvety agacchac chandogo drutaṃ caturikāgṛham / upāviśat praviśyātra kṛtapratyudgatistayā //
english: go to her house.” The Brāhman said: “What am I to do there?” The roué replied: “Give her gold, and in order to please her make use of some sāma”[14] When he heard this, the chanter went quickly to the house of Caturikā; when he entered, the lady advanced to meet him and he took a seat.

sanskrit: māmadya lokayātrāṃ tvaṃ śikṣayaitena sāṃpratam / iti jalpansa tattasyai svarṇamarpitavāndvijaḥ // prahasatyatha tatrasthe jane kiṃcidvicintya saḥ / gokarṇasadṛśau kṛtvā karāvābaddhasāraṇau // tārasvaraṃ tathā sāma gāyati sma jaḍāśayaḥ / yathā tatra milanti sma viṭā hāsyadidṛkṣavaḥ //
english: Then that Brāhman gave her the gold and faltered out the request: “Teach me now for this fee the way of the world.” Thereupon the people who were there began to titter, and he, after reflecting a little, putting his hands together in the shape of a cow’s ear, so that they formed a kind of pipe, began, like a stupid idiot, to chant with a shrill sound the Sāma Veda, so that all the roués in the house came together to see the fun;

sanskrit: te cāvocañ śṛgālo 'yaṃ praviṣṭo 'tra kuto 'nyathā / tac chīghram ardhacandro 'sya gale 'smin dīyatām iti // ardhacandraṃ śaraṃ matvā śiraśchedabhayāddrutam / śikṣitā lokayātreti garjansa niragāttataḥ // tatsakāśaṃ tato 'gacchadyenāsu preṣito 'bhavat / vṛttāntaṃ cāvadattasmai so 'pi cainamabhāṣata //
english: and they said: “Whence has this jackal blundered in here? Come, let us quickly give him the half-moon[15] on his throat.” Thereupon the Brāhman, supposing that the half-moon meant an arrow with a head of that shape, and afraid of having his head cut off, rushed out of the house, bellowing out: “I have learnt the way of the world.” Then he went to the man who had sent him and told him the whole story.

sanskrit: sāma sāntvaṃ mayoktaṃ te vedasyāvasaro 'tra kaḥ / kiṃ vā dhārādhirūḍhaṃ hi jāḍyaṃ vedajaḍe jane // evaṃ vihasya gatvā ca tenoktā sā vilāsinī / dvipadasya paśorasya tatsuvarṇatṛṇaṃ tyaja // hasantyā ca tayā tyaktaṃ suvarṇaṃ prāpya sa dvijaḥ / punarjātamivātmānaṃ manvāno gṛhamāgataḥ //
english: What is the propriety of introducing the Veda in a matter of this kind? The fact is, I suppose, that stupidity is engrained in a man who muddles his head with the Vedas.” So he spoke, bursting with laughter all the while, and went off to the lady’s house and said to her: “Give back to that two-legged cow his gold-fodder.” So she, laughing, gave back the money, and when the Brāhman got it he went back to his house as happy as if he had been born again.

sanskrit: evaṃprāyāṇy ahaṃ paśyan kautukāni pade pade / prāptavān rājabhavanaṃ mahendrasadanopamam //
english: Witnessing strange scenes of this kind at every step, I reached the palace of the king, which was like the Court of Indra.

sanskrit: tataś cāntaḥ praviṣṭo 'haṃ śiṣyair agre niveditaḥ / āsthānasthitamadrākṣaṃ rājānaṃ sātavāhanam // śarvavarmaprabhṛtibhirmantribhiḥ parivāritam / ratnasiṃhāsanāsīnamamarairiva vāsavam //
english: And then I entered it, with my pupils going before to herald my arrival, and saw the King Sātavāhana sitting in his hall of audience upon a jewelled throne, surrounded by his ministers, Śarvavarman and his colleagues, as Indra is by the gods.

sanskrit: vihitasvastikāraṃ māmupaviṣṭamathāsane / rājñā kṛtādaraṃ caiva śarvavarmādayo 'stuvan // ayaṃ deva bhuvi khyātaḥ sarvavidyāviśāradaḥ / guṇāḍhya iti nāmāsya yathārthamata eva hi // ityādi tatstutiṃ dṛṣṭvā mantribhiḥ sātavāhanaḥ / prītaḥ sapadi satkṛtya mantritve māṃ nyayojayat //
english: After I had blessed him and had taken a seat, and had been honoured by the king, Śarvavarman and the other ministers praised me in the following words:— “This man, O king, is famous upon the earth as skilled in all lore, and therefore his name Guṇāḍhya[16] is a true index of his nature.” Sātavāhana, hearing me praised in this style by his ministers, was pleased with me, and immediately entertained me honourably, and appointed me to the office of Minister.

sanskrit: athāhaṃ rājakāryāṇi cintayannavasaṃ sukham / śiṣyānadhyāpayaṃstatra kṛtadāraparigrahaḥ //
english: Then I married a wife, and lived there comfortably, looking after the king’s affairs and instructing my pupils.

sanskrit: kadācitkautukādbhrāmyansvairaṃ godāvarītaṭe / devīkṛtiriti khyātamudyānaṃ dṛṣṭavānaham // taccātiramyamālokya kṣitisthamiva nandanam / udyānapālaḥ pṛṣṭo 'bhūnmayā tatra tadāgamam // sa ca māmabravītsvāminvṛddhebhyaḥ śrūyate yathā / pūrvaṃ maunī nirāhāro dvijaḥ kaścitamāyayau //
english: Once, as I was roaming about at leisure on the banks of the Godāvarī out of curiosity, I beheld a garden called Devīkṛti, and seeing that it was an exceedingly pleasant garden, like an earthly Nandana,[17] I asked the gardener how it came there, and he said to me: “My lord, according to the story which we hear from old people, long ago there came here a certain Brāhman who observed a vow of silence and abstained from food;

sanskrit: sa divyamidamudyānaṃ sadevabhavanaṃ vyadhāt / tato 'tra brāhmaṇāḥ sarve milanti sma sakautukāḥ // nirbandhāttaiḥ sa pṛṣṭaḥ svaṃ vṛttāntam avadad dvijaḥ / astīha bharukacchākhyo viṣayo narmadātaṭe //
english: he made this heavenly garden with a temple; then all the Brāhmans assembled here out of curiosity, and that Brāhman being persistently asked by them told his history: “‘There is in this land a province called Bakakaccha, on the banks of the Narmadā;

sanskrit: tasminn ahaṃ samutpanno viprastasya ca me purā / na bhikṣāmapyadātkaściddaridrasyālasasya ca //
english: in that district I was born as a Brāhman, and in former times no one gave me alms, as I was lazy as well as poor;

sanskrit: atha khedādgṛhaṃ tyaktvā virakto jīvitaṃ prati / bhrāntvā tīrthānyahaṃ draṣṭumagacchaṃ vindhyavāsinīm // dṛṣṭvā tataśca tāṃ devīmiti saṃcintitaṃ mayā / lokaḥ paśūpahāreṇa prīṇāti varadāmimām // ahaṃ tvātmānameveha hanmi mūrkhamimaṃ paśum / niścityeti śiraśchettuṃ mayā śastramagṛhyata //
